articles.title: BudgetMix RL: What Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning Really Improves in LLM Agents
articles.excerpt: BudgetMix RL: What Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning Really Improves in LLM Agents Teams training LLM agents with multi-turn reinforcement learning usually report one number: success rate on a long-ho…
articles.body: BudgetMix RL: What Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning Really Improves in LLM Agents Teams training LLM agents with multi-turn reinforcement learning usually report one number: success rate on a long-horizon benchmark. A new paper, What Does Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning Really Improve in LLM Agents? , asks what sits behind that number. Its answer matters for anyone shipping agents: the gains depend heavily on how many turns the agent is allowed at inference time, and they come from a specific skill, recovering from mistakes. The authors also propose BudgetMix RL, a training change meant to make agents robust when the turn budget shrinks.

articles.title: How to A/B Test AI-Written Cold Emails and Improve Your Reply Rate
articles.excerpt: The fastest way to get value from AI for cold emails is not to ask for one sample and hit send. Ask for two drafts built on different angles, send each to half your list, and use whichever gets more r…
articles.body: The fastest way to get value from AI for cold emails is not to ask for one sample and hit send. Ask for two drafts built on different angles, send each to half your list, and use whichever gets more replies as the base for the next round. Once an AI draft stops being a finished product and becomes something to compare, the whole workflow changes. Plenty of freelancers and small agencies write their own outreach. A common habit is to search for "sales email template," swap in the recipient's name and send. A more reliable routine is to have AI produce two versions, split the list in half, and keep the one that earns replies. This article walks through that improvement loop in a form a single person can actually run.
articles.author: Hanako H.

articles.title: Build vs Buy in Google Sheets: The Break-Even Cell That Said -400 Months
articles.excerpt: Our build-vs-buy guide gives one formula for deciding whether to replace a subscription with your own automation: break-even months = B / (S − R − M). B is the one-time build cost, S the subscription…
articles.body: Our build-vs-buy guide gives one formula for deciding whether to replace a subscription with your own automation: break-even months = B / (S − R − M). B is the one-time build cost, S the subscription per month, R what the build costs to run, M monthly maintenance. In a sheet it is one cell: =B2/(B1-B3-B4) . Run it with a small tool's numbers: 10 seats at $12, a $12,000 build quote, and maintenance at the guide's fallback of 15% of the build a year. The cell comes out at -400 . Put the obvious check next to it, =IF(B5<=36,"BUILD","BUY") , and it says BUILD . Upkeep alone was $150 a month against a $120 subscription, so the build never pays back, and the sheet recommended it anyway.

CrashFlex: Car Crash Simulator (Android and iOS, by Redour) takes a different approach: according to its store listing, every vehicle is built from hundreds of nodes and beams and simulated in real time. The developer says CrashFlex is optimized to keep crashes smooth on mobile. I haven't seen the source, so I can't verify how, but it is a useful example of physics-driven gameplay on mobile hardware.

articles.title: Flush on a Deadline, Not on a Newline: Replacing Line-Buffered Output
articles.excerpt: One byte is quietly taxing almost every command-line program you run: the newline at the end of a log line. Not because the byte itself is expensive, but because of what your C library or language run…
articles.body: One byte is quietly taxing almost every command-line program you run: the newline at the end of a log line. Not because the byte itself is expensive, but because of what your C library or language runtime has promised to do when it sees one. Line buffering turns each completed line into an immediate system call, and when the program prints thousands of lines, that promise turns into thousands of system calls. A recent post by Chris Wellons, writing about his own unzip replacement, makes a sharper claim: we do not have to choose between prompt output and fast output. Flush on a short deadline instead of on a newline, and you get both.

The dream of hosting private, zero-latency, local AI models often feels out of reach, gated by high hardware costs. However, systematic benchmarking across every major computing hardware tier reveals a far more nuanced — and empowering — reality. Deploying local AI is not a binary choice between high-end server clusters and zero local execution.

articles.title: You don't have to go to the moon to see Earth differently: Artemis II astronaut Victor Glover on what really matters
articles.excerpt: After a record-breaking journey around the moon, Artemis 2 astronaut Victor Glover explains why you don't need to travel into space to see Earth differently.
articles.body: TENERIFE, Canary Islands — Imagine traveling over 250 million miles from home, watching Earth disappear behind the moon and losing contact with the billions of people who call it home. What would you miss most? For Artemis II astronaut Victor Glover, the answer wasn't a particular place, a familiar view or even the comforts of home. It was something much more fundamental: human connection. Speaking during a discussion with former astronaut Chris Hadfield at the Starmus VIII festival on Oct. 18 in Tenerife, Canary Islands, Glover reflected on the extraordinary experience of traveling around the moon and how being so far from Earth had given him a renewed appreciation for the people living on it. "The greatest reason to go to space, it isn't to be a swashbuckler hero," Glover said.

articles.excerpt: NASA's Voyager 1 probe is back in communication after the 49-year-old spacecraft briefly fell silent last month, during its interstellar-space mission.
articles.body: Voyager, 1, humanity's most distant spacecraft, is back in contact after briefly losing touch with Earth last month. The spacecraft stopped phoning home for about 48 hours between Oct. 18 and 20 due to a communications glitch that Voyager 1 resolved on its own, before engineers could send the long-running spacecraft a remote fix. "This is the first time we've seen the spacecraft do something like this, but we are also at a point in the mission where we have to expect the unexpected," Kareem Badaruddin, Voyager mission manager at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), said in an agency statement about the incident on Oct. 29.
articles.author: Elizabeth Howell

articles.title: NASA Astronauts to Answer Questions from Florida Students
articles.excerpt: Students in Florida will hear from NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney as they answer prerecorded STEM questions while aboard the International Space Station. The Earth-to-space call will…
articles.body: From left, SpaceX Crew-13 pilot Luke Delaney and commander Jessica Watkins, both NASA astronauts, are pictured in their pressure suits during a training session at SpaceX headquarters in Hawthorne, California. Credit: SpaceX Students in Florida will hear from NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney as they answer prerecorded STEM questions while aboard the  International Space Station . The Earth-to-space call will begin at 10:40 a.m. EST Tuesday, Nov. 10, and will stream live on the agency’s Learn With NASA  YouTube channel. This event is hosted by Freedom Crossing Academy in St. Johns, Florida, for students in grades K-12, and the community. This unique opportunity aims to deepen understanding of space exploration and enhance awareness of STEM careers.

articles.title: Earth photobombs spacewalking Canadian astronaut | Space photo of the day for Nov. 5, 2026
articles.excerpt: Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk poses for a photo mid-spacewalk on Oct. 29, 2026.
articles.body: Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk poses for a photo during his spacewalk on Oct. 29, 2026. (Image credit: CSA) Spacewalks are hard work, so sometimes you need to take a break for a moment and snap a gorgeous selfie with your home planet in the background. What is it? During a pre-Halloween spacewalk on Oct. 29, 2026, Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk took a moment to pose for a photograph. In this moment , the International Space Station to which he was tethered was orbiting 267 miles (430 kilometers) above the South Atlantic Ocean down below on Earth.
